title: 06. Memory, State & HITL: Day 14 — Streaming & UX
summary: A 30-second wait for an LLM response feels broken. A 30-second wait where you watch the answer form token by token feels fast.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
A 30-second wait for an LLM response feels broken. A 30-second wait where you watch the answer form token by token feels fast. Streaming is the single biggest UX upgrade you can make to an agent, and it's also surprisingly easy — both LangChain and Pydantic AI expose streaming primitives that work with any model provider.

Today's projects cover the two main streaming patterns:

1. **Live Email Drafter** (LangChain) — token streaming via `chain.stream()`, rendered to the terminal with `rich.live` so the user watches the email form in real time.
2. **Real-time Meeting Summarizer** (Pydantic AI) — event streaming via `agent.iter()`, which yields every step in the agent loop (model requests, tool calls, response handling) as it happens. The output is structured, so we render it with `rich` panels at the end.

Token streaming is what users see; event streaming is what *you* as a developer see (and what enables progress UIs in production). Knowing both patterns is essential.

sections.title: Common Pitfalls
sections.body:
**Forgetting `streaming=True` on the model.** `chain.stream()` always returns an iterator, but without `streaming=True` on `ChatOpenAI`, each "chunk" is the complete response. You'll see one big print at the end instead of token-by-token streaming. Set the flag explicitly even though some providers default to streaming — being explicit prevents surprises when you swap providers.

**Mixing async and sync.** Pydantic AI's `agent.iter()` is async-only. If you call it from a sync context you'll get `RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop`. Either make your whole call stack async, or use `asyncio.run()` at the entrypoint (as in our `main`). Don't try to mix `agent.run_sync()` with `agent.iter()` in the same codebase — pick one style per file.

**Event type confusion.** `agent.iter()` yields nodes, not strings. Calling `print(node)` on a `ModelRequestNode` dumps a huge `ModelRequest` object to the terminal. Use the `is_model_request_node` and `is_call_tools_node` predicates to dispatch, and only access `.request` or `.response` after the predicate check. Accessing attributes on the wrong node type raises `AttributeError`.

**Buffering kills streaming UX.** If you pipe a streaming script's output to a file (`python script.py > out.txt`), Python detects the non-TTY and buffers stdout — you'll see nothing until the buffer flushes. For demos, run scripts directly in the terminal. For production, set `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1` or call `sys.stdout.flush()` after each chunk.

**`rich.live` refresh rate too high.** Calling `live.update()` on every token can produce 100+ updates per second, which thrashes the terminal. Cap `refresh_per_second=15` (good for human eyes) and let `rich` drop intermediate frames. Your loop runs at full speed; `rich` just samples at 15 fps.

**Async generators not awaited.** `agent.iter()` is an async context manager. Writing `for node in agent.iter(...)` (no `async`) silently iterates nothing. Use `async with agent.iter(...) as run: async for node in run:`. The `async for` is mandatory.

**Structured output + streaming tension.** When `result_type=SomeModel`, the model's response is JSON. You can stream the raw JSON tokens, but you can't safely parse partial JSON. Pydantic AI's `iter()` handles this by giving you node-level events (model request, call tools) rather than raw tokens. If you want token-level streaming with structured output, you have to do the parsing yourself — usually not worth it. For token streaming, use plain text output.

sections.title: Next: Day 15 — Multi-Agent Systems
sections.body: A single agent with tools and memory can do a lot — but some tasks need specialization. Tomorrow you build two multi-agent systems: a Researcher-Writer duo where one agent gathers facts and another writes prose, and a Triage-Respond pipeline where a router agent decides which specialist handles each incoming message. You'll use LangGraph for the orchestration and Pydantic AI for the individual agents, combining everything you've learned in Days 8-14.
